source.citation: Louie, A. H. (2012). Anticipation in (M,R)-systems. International Journal of General Systems 41(1), 5-22.
source.note: Quotes are verbatim from the PDF's text layer. Where a quote contains notation the text layer garbles, the notation is restored and quote_note says so.

claims.label: Postulate of Life: an organism is whatever realizes an (M,R)-system
claims.statement: A natural system is an organism if and only if it realizes an (M,R)-system.
claims.quote: A natural system is an organism if and only if it realizes an (M,R)-system.

formalization.note: A postulate, attributed by Louie to Rosen. It defines its subject and is not provable; it is testable only once 'realizes' is given an operational reading.

claims.label: Metabolic hom-sets are a proper subset of all mappings
claims.statement: The mappings that model metabolic processes, H(A,B), form a proper subset of all mappings B^A from A to B.
claims.quote: Members of H(A,B) are the mappings that model metabolic process, so clearly not all mappings in B^A qualify; thus, H(A,B) is a proper subset of B^A.
claims.quote_note: Notation H(A,B) and B^A restored; the text layer renders them as 'H A; B' and 'B A'.

formalization.note: A modelling stipulation, not a theorem. louie2012-04 shows it is load-bearing: with the full function space, replication never exists (not_replicates_full).

claims.label: Repair maps rebuild the metabolic components
claims.statement: Repair is a mapping whose outputs are metabolic mappings; in the simplest case a repair is a map from B to H(A,B).
claims.quote: Repair may be considered as mappings that create new copies of enzymes

formalization.note: Encoded as the field Rep of RelationalLaws.Replication.Network.

claims.label: Replication comes for free from metabolism and repair, under conditions
claims.statement: In an (M,R)-system A -> B -> H(A,B), a replication map from H(A,B) to H(B,H(A,B)) can be obtained by inverting evaluation at a point b of B, but only under conditions on the mappings involved; replication is not an obligatory feature of repair.
claims.quote: Each entailment of replication from metabolism and repair depends on some 'stringent but not prohibitively strong conditions' imposed on the mapping(s) involved.

readings.name: condition
readings.statement: Replication at b exists if and only if evaluation at b (repair maps to the metabolism they produce at b) is one-to-one on the admissible repairs.

readings.name: restricted-hom-set
readings.statement: With repairs restricted to constant maps, replication exists at every b.

readings.name: full-function-space
readings.statement: With every map B -> H(A,B) admitted as a repair, replication exists.
readings.status: false whenever B has two points and there are two metabolisms (machine-checked counterexample)

formalization.note: The quoted 'stringent conditions' are made exact: injectivity of evaluation, necessary and sufficient. Whether they hold depends on the hom-set reading, which is where encodings of Rosen part. Proved about the model only; nothing here says which reading organisms realize. Letelier et al. (2006, doi:10.1016/j.jtbi.2005.07.007) state the one-to-one condition and the proper-subset requirement informally; this is the machine-checked, necessary-and-sufficient form.

claims.label: Most (M,R)-systems cannot replicate
claims.statement: The conditions for entailment closure will usually not be satisfied, so most (M,R)-systems cannot replicate.
claims.quote: It may be expected that these conditions for 'entailment closure' will not usually be satisfied, and hence that most (M,R)-systems cannot replicate.

formalization.note: 'Most' needs a measure over (M,R)-systems that the source does not give. Under the full-function-space reading, not_replicates_full gives 'none' rather than 'most'; under restricted readings the share depends on the restriction. Open.

claims.label: Replicability is relational, not mechanism-specific
claims.statement: Replicability in an (M,R)-system is a relational result, independent of any particular physical mechanism; nucleic-acid replication is one realization among many.
claims.quote: It is also important to note that replicability is a relational result; i.e. independent of any particular physical mechanism or realization.

claims.label: Metabolism, repair and replication are roles, not kinds
claims.statement: In the chain f, Phi, beta, the last two maps are themselves an (M,R)-system with Phi as metabolism and beta as repair; which map counts as metabolism, repair or replication depends on the system it is read in.
claims.quote: there is nothing intrinsic about the biological qualities of metabolism, repair, and replication; our perception of them depends on the total system in which they are embedded.

formalization.note: Follows from the types alone: a repair B -> H(A,B) is a metabolism A' -> B' with A' = B and B' = H(A,B), and a replication map has the type of a repair one level up.

claims.label: Closure to efficient causation is stricter than containing a causal cycle
claims.statement: Systems closed to efficient causation are a proper subset of systems that contain a closed path of efficient causation.
claims.quote: The class of systems that are closed to efficient causation forms a proper subset of the class of systems that contain a closed path of efficient causation.

readings.name: clef
readings.statement: Closed to efficient causation means every process lies on a hierarchical cycle (a closed path of entailment through at least two processes). Then every such system with a process is complex, and some complex systems are not closed.

readings.name: entailed-within
readings.statement: Closed to efficient causation means every process is entailed by some process of the system. Then closed systems need not be complex.
readings.status: false in general: one self-entailing process, or an infinite regress (machine-checked counterexamples)

readings.name: entailed-within, finite, no self-entailment
readings.statement: Under the entailed-within reading, a finite system in which no process entails itself is complex.

formalization.note: Which of Louie's two definitions of closure (see louie2012-09) is used decides whether the claim holds. Encoding: processes with an entailment relation, g entails f when f is an output of g (hierarchical composition, Louie eq. 18).

claims.label: Two definitions of closure to efficient causation, called equivalent
claims.statement: A system is closed to efficient causation if every efficient cause is entailed within the system; equivalently, if it has a model in which all processes lie on hierarchical cycles.
claims.quote: Definition. A natural system is closed to efficient causation if its every efficient cause is entailed within the system. Equivalently, a closed-to-efficient-cause system has a model in which all processes are involved in hierarchical cycles.

readings.name: clef implies entailed-within
readings.statement: If every process lies on a hierarchical cycle, every process is entailed within the system.

readings.name: entailed-within implies clef, same system
readings.statement: If every process is entailed within a formal system, every process of that same system lies on a hierarchical cycle.
readings.status: false (three-process counterexample: f and g entail each other, f entails h)

formalization.note: Louie states the equivalence for natural systems through the phrase 'has a model', and says it lets the term be used on formal systems. Taken on a single formal system, with the system as its own model, only one direction holds. Whether some other model always restores the equivalence depends on what counts as a model, which the paper does not fix here.

claims.label: The loop closes by identifying each point b with a replication map
claims.statement: Replication becomes entailed within an (M,R)-system by identifying the set B with the set of replication maps H(H(A,B), H(B,H(A,B))), each point b with the inverse of evaluation at b; no new efficient cause is added.
claims.quote: An isomorphic identification between the sets B and H(H(A,B),H(B,H(A,B))) (i.e. between b ∈ B and β) is made – Rosen uses one due to the 'inverse evaluation map' with β = b̂⁻¹.
claims.quote_note: The text layer interleaves this sentence with the one before it and garbles the notation; the quote was checked against the rendered page. The general form, for any three maps in a hierarchy of hom-sets, is on p. 12.

readings.name: full-function-space
readings.statement: Every map H(A,B) -> H(B,H(A,B)) counts as a replication map, and B is identified with all of them.
readings.status: false whenever A is nonempty and B has two points: no map from B reaches them all (Cantor's diagonal argument, machine-checked)

readings.name: restricted-hom-sets
readings.statement: The replication maps are exactly Rosen's inverse evaluations, one per point of B, and the repairs are restricted so that each inverse exists.
readings.status: proved satisfiable: a two-point cell in which the whole loop closes

formalization.note: 'Isomorphic identification between the sets' is read as a bijection. The full-function-space result needs only onto-ness, so it holds for any reading that requires every replication map to be some point of B. If the identification were a mere map, it would itself be an efficient cause needing entailment. Letelier et al. (2006) note informally that the sets must be 'small enough' and that Rosen's full function spaces are 'too big'; Cantor's argument is the exact form of that remark.
